title: Two strangers can agree on a secret while everyone listens in
body: In **Diffie–Hellman key exchange**, two people agree on a public starting value, each mixes in a secret of their own, and they swap the results in the open. Each then mixes their own secret into what they received, and both end up with the same key. An eavesdropper sees everything sent but never the secrets, and with numbers hundreds of digits long, working backwards is far too hard. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published the method in 1976; Britain's GCHQ had found it earlier but kept it secret.

slides.alt: Watercolour animation: Alice and Bob each mix a secret colour into public yellow, swap the jars while Eve's eye watches, and add their secret again to get the same brown. Then the same with numbers: they send 10 and 17 and both reach 14.

slides.prompt: Pick secrets for Alice and Bob: their keys always match. Then play Eve, who sees only the public numbers, and find Alice’s secret.
slides.takeaway: With a small prime Eve just tries every power. Real exchanges use primes over 600 digits long, where trying them all would take longer than the age of the universe.

slides.question: Eve heard 23, 5, 10 and 17. What does she still need to work out the shared key, 14?
options: The order they were sent in
Nothing: she can read it off
slides.explanation: Everything else is public. With either secret she could repeat that person's last step; with tiny numbers she could also just try them all, which is why real keys are enormous.

slides.heading: Easy one way, hard the other
slides.text: Like mixing paint, raising 5 to a power and keeping the remainder is quick. Going back, from the remainder to the secret power, is the discrete logarithm problem: for a large enough prime, no known method on ordinary computers can solve it in practice.

slides.label: the recommended minimum size of the public prime
slides.text: That is a number about 617 digits long. With 23, as in the animation, there are only 23 possible remainders to try.

slides.heading: Oldest first
items: UK codebreakers at GCHQ find the ideas
Diffie and Hellman publish key exchange
Rivest, Shamir and Adleman invent RSA
slides.explanation: GCHQ got there first in the early 1970s but kept it secret; Diffie–Hellman came in 1976, RSA in 1977, and the GCHQ work stayed classified until 1997.

slides.heading: Found twice
slides.text: At Britain's GCHQ, James Ellis imagined “non-secret encryption” in 1970, Clifford Cocks found a way to do it in 1973, and Malcolm Williamson developed this very key exchange in 1974. The British government declassified their work in 1997.

slides.heading: Still everywhere
slides.text: Diffie–Hellman helps secure many internet services. In the ephemeral modes of TLS, the protocol that protects secure websites, a fresh exchange gives every session its own key, so a key stolen later can't unlock past conversations.
